summary: Across the lake, Jesus frees a man held by a legion of demons, lets them enter a herd of swine, and sends the man home as His witness.
key_insight: Three parties beg Jesus in this story: the demons, the townspeople and the healed man. He grants the first two requests and refuses only the man who wants to go with Him. That refusal is a commission: the man becomes Jesus’ witness in the Decapolis.
story: After the storm, Jesus and His disciples came to the other side of the sea, to the country of the Gadarenes, opposite Galilee. {Lk} As soon as Jesus stepped out of the boat, a man with an unclean spirit came out of the tombs to meet Him. {Mk} Matthew tells us there were two such men, so fierce that no one could pass that way. {Mt}

The man had been gripped by demons for a long time. He wore no clothes and lived among the tombs, not in a house. {Lk} People had often bound him with shackles and chains, but he tore the chains apart and broke the shackles in pieces; no one could tame him. Night and day he was in the mountains and in the tombs, crying out and cutting himself with stones. {Mk}

When he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and worshiped Him. He cried out with a loud voice, “What have I to do with You, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I implore You by God that You do not torment me.” For Jesus had said to him, “Come out of the man, unclean spirit!” {Mk} In Matthew the demons ask, “Have You come here to torment us before the time?” {Mt}

Jesus asked, “What is your name?” He answered, “My name is Legion; for we are many.” The demons begged Him not to send them out of the country {Mk} or command them to go into the abyss. {Lk} A large herd of swine, about two thousand, was feeding on the mountainside, and the demons begged, “Send us to the swine, that we may enter them.” {Mk} Jesus said, “Go.” {Mt} The unclean spirits came out and entered the swine, and the whole herd ran violently down the steep place into the sea and drowned.

The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country, and people came out to see what had happened. They found the man who had been possessed sitting at the feet of Jesus, {Lk} clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. When those who had seen it told them about the man and about the swine, {Mk} the whole multitude of the surrounding region asked Jesus to leave them, for they were seized with great fear. {Lk}

As Jesus was getting into the boat, the man begged to go with Him. Jesus did not permit him, but said, “Go home to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you, and how He has had compassion on you.” {Mk} So he went and proclaimed throughout the whole city {Lk} and across the Decapolis all that Jesus had done for him, and all marveled. {Mk}
differences: Matthew tells of two demon-possessed men; Mark and Luke tell of one.
In the NKJV, Matthew calls the place “the country of the Gergesenes”; Mark and Luke call it “the country of the Gadarenes.”
Only Mark and Luke record the name “Legion” and the healed man’s request to go with Jesus. Only Mark gives the number of swine, about two thousand.
Matthew alone records the demons’ words “before the time”; Luke alone mentions “the abyss” and says the man sat “at the feet of Jesus.”

fit.question: Matthew says two demon-possessed men met Jesus. Mark and Luke tell of one. How many were there?

points.label: Two were there
points.text: Matthew counts both men. Mark and Luke follow the one who spoke, who bore the name Legion, and who stayed behind as a witness. Neither of them says there was only one.

points.label: A pattern in Matthew
points.text: Matthew counts two again at Jericho (Matthew 20:30), where Mark names only Bartimaeus. He tends to report everyone present; Mark and Luke focus on the person the story centers on.

fit.note: Telling the story of one man does not deny that a second was there.
fit.short: There were two. Mark and Luke tell the story of the one who spoke and later became a witness; Matthew counts both.

fit.question: The NKJV reads “Gergesenes” in Matthew and “Gadarenes” in Mark and Luke, and many modern translations read Gerasenes. Where did this happen?

points.label: Copies differ
points.text: Hand-copied manuscripts of all three Gospels vary among these similar-sounding names. The NKJV follows one family of manuscripts; other translations follow older copies, which read Gadarenes in Matthew and Gerasenes in Mark and Luke.

points.label: A district and a town
points.text: Gadara was a well-known city of the Decapolis about six miles southeast of the lake, and its lands probably reached the shore. The large city of Gerasa lay over thirty miles away, too far for the swine’s rush into the sea, so the names Gerasa and Gergesa likely point to a small lakeside town. Edersheim and McGarvey both placed it at the ruins called Kersa (today Kursi), on the eastern shore, near a steep slope that runs close to the water.

points.label: Like a city and a suburb
points.text: A place can be named for the main city of its district or for the village nearby, the way a modern writer might name a county or a town.

fit.note: Similar names, copied by hand and used for a district and a town, all point to the same stretch of eastern shore; nothing here requires an error.
fit.short: Gadara was the district’s main city; Gergesa (Kursi) a lakeside town. Copies vary among the similar names, but all point to the eastern shore.

scene.label: Unclean ground
scene.text: Jesus stepped ashore among things a devout Jew avoided: Gentile country, tombs (touching the dead made a person unclean, Numbers 19:11) and pigs, which the Law called unclean (Leviticus 11:7).

scene.label: Rock tombs
scene.text: The hills along the eastern shore are full of caves and tombs cut into the rock. A man driven out of town could live there, among the dead, out of everyone’s way.

scene.label: “Legion”
scene.text: A Roman legion was a unit of several thousand soldiers. In a land held by Roman troops, the name meant a vast, organized force, and Luke explains it: “many demons had entered him.”

scene.label: The Decapolis
scene.text: The “Ten Cities” were Greek-style towns, most of them east of the Jordan, with Gentile temples, theaters and markets. Few people there kept the Law of Moses, so herding pigs was ordinary business.

scene.label: “Most High God”
scene.text: The demon calls Jesus “Son of the Most High God.” Scripture often uses this name for God where Gentiles are involved (Genesis 14:18; Daniel 4:2; Acts 16:17), and it fits a scene outside Israel.

witnesses.matthew: Tells it in seven verses and counts both men. In Matthew’s chain of miracles (chapters 8–9) it shows the King’s authority over demons, who know a time of judgment is coming and fear that He has brought it early.
witnesses.mark: Gives the fullest and most vivid account: chains snapped, cutting with stones, about two thousand swine, a man sent home to the Decapolis. Mark places it between the stilling of the storm and the raising of Jairus’s daughter, so Jesus is shown as Lord over the sea, demons, disease and death in quick succession.
witnesses.luke: Adds that the man wore no clothes, had been kept under guard and dreaded the abyss. Luke alone says he sat “at the feet of Jesus,” the place of a disciple (compare Mary in Luke 10:39), and ends with him telling his whole city what Jesus had done.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is stronger than a whole legion of evil. The demons recognize Him, plead with Him and cannot move without His word, yet He gives His full attention to one man no chain could hold and no one could help.
seeing.living: Jesus did not take this man on the road with Him; He sent him back to the people who had known him at his worst. “Go home to your friends.” The first place to tell what He has done may be the place where everyone remembers what you were.
seeing.ponder: Who knew you before Jesus found you, and have you told them what great things He has done for you?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus frees the man no one could tame and sends him home to tell it.
outline: A man no one could bind (1–5)
A Lord the demons must obey (6–13)
A town that asked Him to leave (14–17)
preaching.watch_for: Jesus told the man to tell what “the Lord” had done for him (5:19). Mark says he went and proclaimed what “Jesus” had done (5:20). The man’s witness quietly identifies Jesus with the Lord.
related_other: Psalm 107:10–16 · He broke their chains in pieces
Luke 10:17–20 · Even the demons are subject to us
